body_paragraphs: LeBron's decision took seven weeks of speculation and about as long as a text message to actually land: Philadelphia, not Miami, not Cleveland. Kalshi had the Heat as betting favorite Friday morning; by afternoon, Rich Paul was telling ESPN that James chose to protect the memory of a title already won rather than risk a second act. Miami's roster is settled now, the question answered without them. The Marlins have no equivalent resolution: eleven straight losses tied the franchise's worst skid since June 2011, and a team that sat ten games over .500 on July 9 is back to breakeven the hard way. Today's finale against the Padres decides whether it gets worse.

The war changed shape this week more than it ended. Direct U.S. strikes on Iran paused Friday night after thirteen consecutive nights, but the Houthis opened a new front Saturday, hitting Saudi Aramco facilities in Jizan and Yanbu hard enough to read as retaliation, not de-escalation. Oil eased off its $100 peak on the pause; whether Saturday undoes that is a Monday question. The Fed meets Tuesday and Wednesday with hike odds still near 34%, an odd place to be after a month spent insisting inflation was cooling. Closer to home, Witkoff and Monroe Capital closed $303 million to break ground on the old Miami Arena site downtown, proof capital still moves on the right deals even as South Florida sales volume runs 13% below last year.

Nothing came in from you this week - no stars, no saves, no notes - so every weight just drifted toward its baseline: Markets and Miami eased slightly, Sports ticked back up, Art of Living settled too. Nothing dramatic, just the system waiting on a signal, not inventing one. The reading list is empty, which is a clean slate, not a backlog. If you have twenty-some minutes this weekend, Skye Cleary's reread of Sartre's Existentialism Is a Humanism is a genuinely different register than the Stoicism this paper usually leans on. And if you're near Miami Beach today, Etel Adnan's ceramic mural comes down from The Bass tonight, for good.

themes.title: LeBron picks Philadelphia, and Miami's summer gets its answer
themes.thesis: The betting favorite lost the bet - LeBron chose to protect a memory instead.
themes.synthesis: LeBron James signed a two-year, $8 million contract with the Philadelphia 76ers on Friday, ending a three-team race that also included Miami and Cleveland, with Golden State floated as a dark horse. Klutch Sports' Rich Paul told ESPN's Ramona Shelburne he initially thought James was headed to Miami, but James ultimately chose not to risk a return to a place where the memory of what he'd already won might not survive a lesser encore. Bronny is not part of the move; James called it his 'last decision,' framed around one more legitimate championship run rather than money. He later posted 'forever love' for the cities that recruited him, Miami included. Heat president Pat Riley, whose relationship with James had reportedly thawed in recent years, said the team was disappointed but moves forward with its roster as built.
themes.new_today: The signing itself, the contract terms, and Rich Paul's account of why Philadelphia won out - all confirmed since Friday morning's edition, which still had Miami as the 51% Kalshi favorite.
themes.why_it_matters: This was the last unresolved question hanging over the Heat's offseason; with it answered, the post-Giannis roster is what it is heading into camp, with no further scrambling for cap space.

themes.title: The strikes on Iran pause; the war doesn't
themes.thesis: A quiet night in Iran came with a loud one in Saudi Arabia - this conflict is relocating, not ending.
themes.synthesis: The US carried out no new strikes on Iran overnight Friday into Saturday, the first pause since the ceasefire collapsed after 13 consecutive nights of strikes, as an Omani diplomatic delegation arrived in Tehran to discuss managing Strait of Hormuz shipping traffic. But Saturday, Iran-aligned Houthi rebels fired dozens of ballistic missiles and drones at Saudi Aramco facilities in Jizan and Yanbu, setting large fires across an industrial area anchored by a major oil refinery - widely read as retaliation for Saudi strikes on a Houthi-held coastal city in Yemen. Brent crude, which topped $100 Thursday for the first time since May, eased to about $96.80 Friday, down nearly 4% on the day but still up more than 12% on the week. Trump had signaled Friday that talks with Iran were 'getting more serious'; an Iranian official dismissed the suggestion hours later.
themes.new_today: The overnight pause itself, the Omani delegation, and the new Houthi strikes on Saudi Aramco facilities - all developments since Friday morning's edition.
themes.why_it_matters: A pause in one theater doesn't mean de-escalation if the fight just moved to Saudi oil infrastructure; Monday's oil pricing is the real test of how markets read this weekend.

themes.title: Fed week arrives with hike odds still historically high
themes.thesis: Two days out, the market still can't decide if this is a hike meeting.
themes.synthesis: The FOMC meets Tuesday and Wednesday, with a decision due 2 PM Wednesday and a press conference from Fed Chair Kevin Warsh to follow. CME FedWatch had hike odds at roughly 34% (66% hold) heading into the weekend, down slightly from Thursday's post-selloff spike near 36.5% but still far above where the month started. Friday's session was mixed - the S&P edged up 0.05% to 7,412, the Nasdaq fell 0.64% to 24,976 on continued tech weakness, and the Dow rose 0.46% - while the 10-year Treasury held essentially flat at 4.69%, just off Thursday's highest close since January 2025.
themes.new_today: Friday's actual closing numbers and the eased-but-still-elevated hike odds, confirmed since Thursday's sharper selloff.
themes.why_it_matters: Hike odds this high, this close to a meeting, is not where the Fed wanted to be after months of framing inflation as under control - the oil shock did that on its own.

themes.title: Eleven straight, and a season that flipped in two weeks
themes.thesis: A team ten games over .500 on July 9 is now fighting not to set a franchise-worst record.
themes.synthesis: Miami dropped both weekend games to San Diego - 4-2 Friday, 7-2 Saturday, with Ty France driving in three - extending the losing streak to 11, tying the franchise record last matched in June 2011 and reached only twice before that. The Marlins fell to 52-52, their first .500 record since June 19, a stunning reversal from July 9, when they sat 10 games over .500 and on pace for an 89-win season. Today's series finale against the Padres, first pitch 1:40 PM at loanDepot Park, decides whether Miami snaps the streak or sets a new franchise worst at 12.
themes.new_today: Saturday's loss, the tied franchise record, and today's stakes - all developments since Friday morning's nine-game-streak edition.
themes.why_it_matters: This has moved past a bad stretch inside a playoff race into genuine franchise history, the wrong kind - worth watching today less for the standings than for how a clubhouse responds to a real crisis of confidence.

themes.title: $303 million breaks ground where the old Miami Arena stood
themes.thesis: A marquee construction loan says the CRE slowdown is about selectivity, not a closed spigot.
themes.synthesis: Witkoff, in partnership with Monroe Capital, secured a $303 million loan from Athene Annuity and Life Company and J.P. Morgan Chase to begin construction on the first phase of 700 North Miami Avenue, part of the Miami Worldcenter development. The financing refinances about $57.3 million in existing debt and provides $245.3 million in new construction funding for an 894-unit residential tower with over 17,000 square feet of retail and a nine-story, 167,000-square-foot parking garage. Three more towers, designed by Kobi Karp and rising 50 to 53 stories, are planned for the same nearly five-acre site, once home to the Miami Arena, the Heat's original venue, demolished in 2008. The loan lands the same week South Florida commercial sales volume is running down 13% year over year to $5.42 billion in the first half of 2026.
themes.new_today: The loan closing and its terms are new since last tracked; the South Florida H1 volume figure adds local specificity to the national CBRE data already in this edition's threads.
themes.why_it_matters: Directly in Alex's lane: a top-tier sponsor still finding construction debt at scale on a well-located site is the clearest read on where lenders' actual risk appetite sits right now, more useful than any aggregate volume number.

themes.title: Basquiat's Caribbean lines, on view through next summer
themes.thesis: Ten Basquiat works, on loan from a single collector, are a rare chance to see the artist's Haitian and Puerto Rican inheritance up close.
themes.synthesis: Basquiat: Figures, Signs, Symbols opened June 25 at Perez Art Museum Miami, drawing nine paintings and one sculpture from Ken Griffin's collection - the largest Basquiat presentation Florida has seen. The show, co-curated by Franklin Sirmans and Megan Kincaid, centers on Basquiat's use of portraiture, script, and language; among the works on view is Untitled (Tenant) (1982), a 74-by-96-inch acrylic and oil stick canvas. Basquiat's father was Haitian and his mother Puerto Rican, and that dual heritage runs through the show's language and symbol-driven pieces in ways rarely assembled at this scale outside New York.
themes.new_today: Not new this week, but newly relevant: with the exhibition running through June 2027, this is a standing recommendation rather than a closing-soon alert.
themes.why_it_matters: Miami's Caribbean and Latin American character shows up in its art collections as much as its restaurants; this is one of the more direct expressions of it on view right now.

rabbit_hole.title: Re-reading Sartre's Lecture Existentialism Is a Humanism
rabbit_hole.creator: Skye Cleary, Aeon
rabbit_hole.why: Cleary revisits Sartre's 1945 defense of radical freedom - that we are not born with a fixed nature but define ourselves entirely through what we choose to do. It's a genuinely different philosophical register than the Stoicism this paper usually reaches for, worth the full sit precisely because it argues the opposite instinct: not acceptance, but responsibility for everything, including what feels forced.

beautiful_thing.title: Untitled (ceramic mural)
beautiful_thing.creator: Etel Adnan
beautiful_thing.body: At The Bass in Miami Beach, Etel Adnan's ceramic mural is built from 165 individual tiles, each 16 by 16 inches, assembled into a single work roughly 173 by 260 inches overall - the only mural of its kind by Adnan in the United States. Adnan, a Lebanese-American poet and painter who worked well into her nineties, conceived the piece from a 2020 sketch; its blocks of saturated color and simplified forms carry the same economy as her small oil-on-canvas landscapes, scaled up to architecture. Tonight is the last chance to see it - the installation, paired with new work by Sarah Crowner, closes for good after today.

daily_puzzle.prompt: Three editors closed out last night's paper - Reyes, Voss, and Kim - each responsible for a different section (Markets, Sports, Culture), and each leaving the building at a different hour (6, 8, or 10 PM). Kim closed the Markets section. Whoever left at 6 PM closed Sports. Reyes left later than Voss. Kim left before Reyes. Who closed which section, and when did each leave?
daily_puzzle.hint: Start with Kim's section, then ask what would have to be true if Reyes had closed Sports.
daily_puzzle.solution: Voss closed Sports and left at 6 PM. Kim closed Markets and left at 8 PM. Reyes closed Culture and left at 10 PM.
daily_puzzle.explanation: Kim has Markets from the first clue. If Reyes had closed Sports, the second clue would put Reyes at 6 PM - but the third clue requires Voss to leave earlier than Reyes, and nothing leaves before 6. So Voss closed Sports and left at 6, leaving Reyes with Culture. The last clue then fixes Kim at 8 and Reyes at 10.
